documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

68-year-old retired school librarian transferring care; her previous internist retired. Wants a doctor she can reach by text.

Cardiac history: paroxysmal AF picked up in 2019 after a few trips to the ED with a racing heart. Outside cardiology put her on amiodarone after those visits and she has been on it since, along with metoprolol and digoxin. Warfarin since 2019 (INRs were done at her old office; last one she recalls was "in range"). Told she has a weak heart pump; she thinks the number was 35%. Records requested. Takes furosemide every morning, weight is stable, sleeps on two pillows but says that is habit.

Neuro: Parkinson's, on benztropine 1 mg twice a day for years, followed by an outside neurologist. Brother also has PD.

BP history: hypertension for a long time, never on a dedicated BP pill beyond what she takes for the heart.

PMH also: pneumonia as a teenager, nothing since. No asthma.
PSH: none.
Meds: warfarin 5 mg daily (adjusted per INR), metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, amiodarone 200 mg daily, digoxin 0.125 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, benztropine 1 mg BID.
Allergies: sulfa drugs (rash).
FH: father emphysema (heavy smoker), stroke at 72. Mother CHF, seasonal allergies. Brother PD. Paternal grandfather AF.
SH: lives in Belchertown. Never smoked. Wine on weekends, 2-3 glasses. Retired from a high school library; teaches a community weather class and keeps a cloud journal.
COVID vaccine x2 (Pfizer) this winter.

Exam: vitals as charted. Thin, pleasant, mild resting tremor of the right hand. Heart irregularly irregular at times today, rate controlled, no murmur. Lungs clear. No JVD. Trace ankle edema at most. Skin warm.

A/P
1. Paroxysmal AF on amiodarone, metoprolol, digoxin; warfarin. INR today; the practice will take over INR management, goal 2-3. Digoxin level, TSH and CMP today since she is on amiodarone.
2. HFrEF, EF ~35% by her report. Euvolemic. Continue furosemide. Get the echo.
3. PD: per neurology.
4. HTN: BP fine today.
5. Health maintenance: hep C screen today. Will look at old records for colonoscopy and mammogram dates.
RTC 3 months, INR monthly.

reports.text: Outside study. Left ventricle mildly dilated with global hypokinesis. Estimated LVEF 35%. Right ventricle normal in size and function. No significant valvular stenosis. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Reduced left ventricular systolic function, LVEF 35%.

reports.text: Outside study obtained for palpitations. Lungs clear. Heart size within normal limits. No effusion or pneumothorax.
Outside study. Scattered fibroglandular densities. No suspicious mass, calcification or architectural distortion.

orders.reason: Progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough on amiodarone

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: cough, breathless.

The cough she mentioned in July has not gone away. Dry, persistent, gets in the way of talking. Short of breath going up the little hill behind her house and carrying groceries in from the car; she has been taking shorter evening walks. This has been creeping up over several months. Has lost a little weight without meaning to (down about 1.7 kg since April). No fever, no sweats at night. No wheeze. No leg swelling. OTC cough syrup did nothing.

Meds: still on amiodarone 200 mg daily since 2019, plus metoprolol, digoxin, furosemide, warfarin, benztropine. Allergies: sulfa drugs (rash).

Exam: vitals as charted. Speaks in full sentences, coughs a few times during the visit. RRR. Lungs without wheeze. No JVD. No edema.

A/P: Subacute progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough in a woman on long-term amiodarone. Amiodarone lung toxicity has to be ruled out; heart failure less likely with a stable weight and no edema. Referring to pulmonology, asked for the next available slot. Called her cardiologist's office to let them know. Return precautions reviewed.

documents.title: Pulmonology Consultation
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
Outside pulmonary and critical care group. Date of consultation 2021-09-20.

Reason for referral: progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough.

Ms. Walsh is a 68-year-old never smoker with paroxysmal AF on amiodarone since 2019. For several months her breathing has steadily worsened: she pauses partway up her driveway, stops to catch her breath after making the bed, and the cough comes on with laughing or reading aloud. She had to cancel a talk she was to give for her community weather class. With exertion she gets a dull band of tightness across the lower chest that is not sharp, not positional, and settles with rest. She uses an extra pillow for comfort. Her weight has drifted down a little and her energy is lower. She denies wheeze, fever, night sweats, pleuritic pain, leg swelling, heartburn, postnasal drip, hoarseness and joint pain. She has noticed a faint blue-gray tint on sun-exposed skin and some halos around lights at night. Over-the-counter cough remedies have not helped. No new medicines besides occasional acetaminophen.

Exposures: no occupational dust, no mining or stone work, no birds, no pets. Never smoked. Some wildfire smoke drifted through last summer, but the symptoms started before that. Remote pneumonia as a teenager; no asthma or tuberculosis. A chest film last year for palpitations was normal.

Medications: amiodarone 200 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, digoxin 0.125 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, warfarin, benztropine 1 mg BID. Allergy: sulfa drugs (rash).
Family history: father emphysema (heavy smoker) and stroke; mother CHF and seasonal allergies.

Studies today: chest radiograph shows bilateral reticulonodular opacities with honeycombing. Spirometry shows a restrictive pattern.

Impression: amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity, with a fibrotic component.

Plan:
1. Amiodarone stopped today. I spoke with her cardiologist, who will manage rhythm with metoprolol and digoxin.
2. Prednisone 40 mg daily, then a slow taper over roughly six months; written schedule given.
3. Watch glucose and blood pressure on steroids.
4. Return in about 3 months.

Sleeping less well on the steroid. Amiodarone removed from her med list. Reminded her the INR may move now that amiodarone is out; INR next week. Keep the October visit.

documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group, visit 2022-03-11.

Ms. Walsh, 69, with paroxysmal AF, is seen about six months after her pulmonary evaluation, when amiodarone was stopped for lung toxicity. For two months she has had palpitations, has lost weight without trying and feels more anxious. She notes no change in bowels and no heat or cold intolerance. She finished her prednisone taper on 3/4.

Exam: heart rate 102. Fine tremor of the outstretched hands. Thyroid diffusely enlarged, no nodules felt.
Labs today: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 3 ng/dL, free T3 5.5 pg/mL.

Medications: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, digoxin 0.125 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, warfarin, benztropine 1 mg BID. Allergy: sulfa (rash).

Impression: amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis, arising months after the drug was stopped, which is in keeping with its long tissue half-life.
Plan: urgent endocrinology referral placed. Continue metoprolol. Note that warfarin sensitivity can rise while she is thyrotoxic; INRs should be checked more often for now.

documents.title: Same-Day Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Texted this morning: two days of nausea and vomiting, not eating much, and she is seeing halos around the lights. Seen same day.

70-year-old with paroxysmal AF and HFrEF on digoxin 0.125 mg daily, warfarin, furosemide 40, metoprolol, benztropine. Amiodarone stopped in 2021 (lung toxicity, then thyrotoxicosis). No new medicines. No diarrhea, no abdominal pain, no fever. Keeping fluids down in sips.
Allergies: sulfa drugs (rash).

Exam: BP 130/80, HR 60, RR 16. Looks tired but not toxic. Mucous membranes slightly dry. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Mild pedal edema on both sides. Otherwise unremarkable.

Office ECG: sinus rhythm with occasional PVCs.
Stat labs (back 1:15 pm): digoxin 2.5 ng/mL, potassium 4.5, creatinine 1.2, INR 2.3.

A/P: Digoxin toxicity: GI symptoms and visual halos with a level of 2.5; creatinine 1.2 likely reduced clearance. Hemodynamically fine, no high-grade block or dangerous arrhythmia, potassium normal, so no antidote needed. Hold digoxin. Repeat digoxin level and BMP Tuesday. Called her cardiologist's office with the results. Strict ED precautions for fainting, slow or racing pulse, or worsening vomiting; she has my cell.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Outside emergency department record, visit 2024-05-09.

71-year-old woman with paroxysmal AF on warfarin, systolic heart failure, Parkinson's disease, and past amiodarone lung toxicity, thyrotoxicosis and digoxin toxicity, arriving with four hours of sudden, severe pain in the right eye and blurred vision, with nausea and vomiting.
Medications per patient: benztropine; also warfarin, metoprolol succinate, digoxin, furosemide (outside list also shows amiodarone 200 mg). Allergy: sulfa drugs (rash).

Exam: right eye red with conjunctival injection, cornea hazy, pupil mid-dilated and unreactive to light, visual acuity reduced on the right. Intraocular pressure 48 mmHg right, 14 mmHg left. Fundus poorly seen through the corneal edema.

Impression: acute angle-closure glaucoma, right eye.
ED course: timolol, apraclonidine and pilocarpine drops to the right eye; IV mannitol. Acetazolamide held because of the sulfa allergy. Antiemetic given. Ophthalmology saw her in the department and will perform laser iridotomy in the morning. Discharged to ophthalmology follow-up.

medications.sig: Instill 1 drop in the right eye 4 times daily for 1 week

documents.title: Ophthalmology Letter
documents.author: ophthalmology
documents.body:
Outside ophthalmology. Visits 2024-05-10, 2024-05-11 and 2024-05-24.

Seen from the ED with acute angle closure of the right eye. Laser peripheral iridotomy right eye on 5/10, uncomplicated. Next day the right IOP was 15 mmHg and the cornea had cleared. Prednisolone acetate 1% four times a day to the right eye for one week. On 5/24 a prophylactic laser iridotomy was done on the left eye, which had a narrow angle; both iridotomies are open.

Her benztropine may be continued now that both iridotomies are patent. She has a visually significant cataract in the right eye and we have discussed lens surgery this summer as the definitive step.
Allergy: sulfa (rash).

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Outside emergency department, visit 2025-05-21.

72-year-old woman, past amiodarone and digoxin toxicity, with two hours of palpitations and light-headedness.
Triage: BP 130/85, heart rate 150 and irregular, RR 18.
She says she takes her medicines faithfully, including furosemide, digoxin and warfarin. Home list (outside record): metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, amiodarone 200 mg daily, benztropine 1 mg BID. Allergy: sulfa drugs (rash).
Labs: potassium 3.0 mEq/L, magnesium 1.2 mg/dL, calcium 9.2 mg/dL, digoxin 1.5 ng/mL, INR 2.5.
ECG: ventricular tachycardia.

Course: sustained wide-complex tachycardia with ongoing light-headedness, managed as unstable. Procedural sedation and synchronized cardioversion, one shock, to sinus rhythm. IV potassium and magnesium replacement. Admitted to cardiology telemetry.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside hospital, cardiology service. Admitted 2025-05-21, discharged 2025-05-23.

Diagnosis: ventricular tachycardia, treated with synchronized cardioversion, in the setting of hypokalemia (3.0) and hypomagnesemia (1.2) on loop diuretic.
Course: no recurrence on telemetry after electrolytes were replaced. Echo: LVEF 35%, unchanged. Digoxin level 1.5, within range; digoxin continued. Because the arrhythmia had a reversible cause, an ICD was not recommended at this time.
Discharge medications: potassium chloride 20 mEq daily (new), magnesium oxide 400 mg daily (new), metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, digoxin 0.125 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, warfarin per INR, benztropine 1 mg BID.
Follow-up: primary care within one week with BMP and magnesium; cardiology in 4 weeks.

events.reason: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain and light-headedness

reports.text: Portable AP view. Lungs without new consolidation, effusion or pneumothorax. Heart size within normal limits.
Sinus tachycardia. New right bundle branch block compared with prior.
CT pulmonary angiogram. Large filling defects in the right and left main pulmonary arteries extending into the lobar branches. Right ventricle dilated, RV larger than LV. No pleural effusion.
reports.conclusion: Large bilateral central pulmonary emboli with right ventricular dilation.

documents.title: ICU Discharge Summary
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
Outside hospital, pulmonary and critical care. Admitted 2026-05-06, discharged 2026-05-13.

Presentation: 73-year-old woman four days after a total hip replacement developed sudden shortness of breath, chest pain and light-headedness while walking to the bathroom at home. Background: paroxysmal AF, LV dysfunction, past amiodarone pulmonary toxicity and thyrotoxicosis, past digoxin toxicity. Warfarin had been held for surgery and restarted after it.
On arrival: BP 85/50, HR 110, RR 28, SpO2 89% on room air. Anxious, sweating. Jugular venous distension. Lungs without crackles. No leg swelling or calf tenderness.
Labs: troponin I 0.04 ng/mL, D-dimer 780 ng/mL FEU, BNP 200 pg/mL, INR 1.8.
Chest x-ray unremarkable. ECG: new right bundle branch block.
Home medications per admission list: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, amiodarone 200 mg daily, digoxin 0.125 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, benztropine 1 mg BID, warfarin. Allergy: sulfa drugs (rash).

Diagnosis: massive pulmonary embolism.
Course: CT pulmonary angiogram showed large bilateral central emboli with a dilated right ventricle. Heparin infusion started. Given surgery four days earlier, systemic thrombolysis was avoided and she went for catheter-directed mechanical thrombectomy the same day, with prompt improvement in blood pressure. Vasopressor stopped and room air reached within 3 days. Warfarin resumed with heparin overlap until INR 2-3.

Discharge medications: warfarin (dosed by our anticoagulation clinic), metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, digoxin 0.125 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, benztropine 1 mg BID, potassium chloride 20 mEq daily, magnesium oxide 400 mg daily, acetaminophen as needed.
Follow-up: hospital anticoagulation clinic for INR until her primary care visit; pulmonology in 6-8 weeks; orthopedics as scheduled.
